section_summary: This section opens with three American Embassy despatches and two State Department memoranda documenting hostile or derogatory cartoons of President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull published by the Japan Times and Advertiser in late 1940 and early 1941. It then contains an October 1941 embassy index and the associated Japan Advertiser clippings, which promote Japanese wartime arguments about Anglo-American policy, economic sanctions, China, Thailand, and Japan’s expansion in East and Southeast Asia. The clippings present sanctions and Allied diplomacy as threats while advocating the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere and further Japanese southward advance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5196: Transmitting a Copy of a Cartoon Which Appeared in the Japan Times and Advertiser on December 10, 1940
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a Japan Times and Advertiser cartoon caricaturing Roosevelt alongside Matsuoka, Ribbentrop, Ciano, and Franco.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes a cartoon showing Matsuoka, Ribbentrop, and Ciano leading a child representing Franco while Roosevelt offers the child a money bag. Although he advises against protesting to the Japanese Foreign Ministry, he preserves the cartoon for possible use if Japan later objects to American caricatures of the emperor. Page 3 is the enclosed December 10 cartoon, titled “At It Again.”

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5229
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records that Tokyo despatch No. 5229 transmitted a derogatory cartoon of Roosevelt for possible use in answering Japanese protests.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes the embassy's December 21, 1940 despatch. It notes that the enclosed cartoon might be retained in case the Japanese Embassy protested against American caricatures of the emperor.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5229: Transmitting a Cartoon from the Japan Times and Advertiser of December 16, 1940
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits another caricature of Roosevelt for use if Japan objects to American press treatment of its chief of state.
subfiles.summary: Referring to despatch No. 5196, Grew encloses a second hostile cartoon of Roosevelt. It depicts the president holding the god of war on a leash that he appears barely willing to restrain. Page 7 reproduces the December 16 cartoon, titled “Not Too Anxious to Hold Him Back.”

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5334
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes an embassy despatch enclosing cartoons of Roosevelt and the secretary of state.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Tokyo despatch No. 5334 of February 1, 1941. It says the cartoons were submitted for possible use against future Japanese complaints about American depictions of the emperor.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5334: Transmitting Cartoons of the President and of the Secretary of State Which Appeared in the Japan Times and Advertiser During January 1941
subfiles.doc_type: diplomatic despatch with four newspaper-cartoon enclosures
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards four January 1941 cartoons caricaturing Roosevelt and Cordell Hull.
subfiles.summary: Grew submits three cartoons of Roosevelt and one of Secretary of State Cordell Hull as a matter of record. He again suggests that the material may be useful if the Japanese Embassy protests American caricatures of the emperor or other senior Japanese officials. The enclosures are “The Angel of Peace Taken for a Ride,” “Liberty: 1941 Edition,” “The Bird for a Bribe,” and “America's Great Illusion Act.”

subfiles.title: Summary for Clippings from the Japanese Press, September 1 to October 1, 1941
subfiles.about: Lists fourteen selected Japan Advertiser articles concerning foreign relations, war, politics, and labor.
subfiles.summary: The embassy index organizes the clippings by relations with the United States, China, Thailand, the yen bloc, international affairs, internal politics, and labor. Its subjects include Roosevelt's naval policy, Seigo Nakano's speech, asset freezing, the Changsha campaign, Thai defenses, settlement in yen, and Japanese southward expansion. The subsequent pages contain eleven of the listed articles.

subfiles.title: British, American Policy Seen at Odds with Differences Arising on Far East Issue
subfiles.from: Japan Advertiser, citing a Nichi Nichi dispatch from Shanghai
subfiles.about: Argues that conflicting British and American aims weaken their joint policy toward Japan and Chongqing.
subfiles.summary: The article claims Britain and the United States are competing for postwar advantage and differ over Chongqing, Thailand, French Indochina, Singapore, and the South Pacific. It portrays Britain as anxious to draw America into the European war while Washington allegedly seeks to replace British influence in China. The reported Konoe message to Roosevelt is presented as a threat to Chongqing's position.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt Makes Law
subfiles.about: Condemns Roosevelt's naval policy as an unauthorized declaration of American rights and undeclared war.
subfiles.summary: The editorial interprets Roosevelt's orders against German submarines and surface vessels as active American participation in the war. It asserts that his expansive definition of defensive waters and freedom of the seas repudiates traditional blockade law. The article concludes that the United States is already at war and that Roosevelt's policy is “short of peace.”

subfiles.title: Anglo-U.S. Leaders Given Stiff Answer from Seigo Nakano
subfiles.from: Japan Advertiser, reporting a speech by Seigo Nakano
subfiles.about: Reports Nakano's denunciation of Roosevelt and Churchill and his defense of Japan's Axis-aligned foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Nakano accuses Britain and the United States of using conquest, intimidation, economic pressure, and appeasement to preserve their world position. He declares that Japan will retain the Tripartite Alliance and construct a Greater East Asia Mutual Prosperity Sphere despite Anglo-American demands. He also attacks the Atlantic declaration as an effort to revive the Versailles order and perpetuate Anglo-American control.

subfiles.title: Anglo-U.S. Freezing of Japanese Assets Proves Boomerang to America, Britain
subfiles.from: Japan Advertiser, citing the Nichi Nichi
subfiles.about: Claims Anglo-American asset freezes harmed British and American interests in East Asia more than Japan.
subfiles.summary: Using reports from Shanghai, Hong Kong, Hanoi, Guangzhou, Bangkok, and Manila, the article describes currency instability, shortages, inflation, and declining Anglo-American commercial influence. It claims the sanctions disrupted Hong Kong and the Dutch East Indies while encouraging Shanghai's integration into Japan's proposed regional economic sphere. The clipping also includes a report on the delayed British evacuation ship Anhui at Yokohama and an incidental Domei item on Brazil's suspension of yarn exports.

subfiles.title: Shanghai Rumors
subfiles.about: Accuses Chongqing agents and foreign correspondents in Shanghai of spreading false reports about Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial says sensational Shanghai reporting misrepresents Japanese troop movements, domestic conditions, Soviet-Japanese relations, and relations with the United States. It portrays Chongqing agents as planting stories intended to provoke conflict and urges foreign governments and newspapers to restrain or scrutinize such reporting. It warns that Japan may take protective measures if Shanghai's foreign privileges facilitate hostile propaganda.

subfiles.title: Taking Changsha Is Master Stroke
subfiles.about: Presents the Japanese capture of Changsha as a decisive operational victory over the Chinese Ninth War Zone.
subfiles.summary: The article describes Japanese crossings of rivers and fortified terrain, the encirclement of Chinese armies, and entry into Changsha on September 27. It attributes the victory to surprise, coordinated detachments, naval and air support, and the concentration of Chinese forces in positions vulnerable to encirclement. The account predicts the destruction of Chiang Kai-shek's Ninth War Zone and the weakening of Chinese resistance.

subfiles.title: That Vulnerable Front
subfiles.about: Argues that political divisions and dependence on foreign support make the Chongqing front vulnerable to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial reviews conflict between the Kuomintang and Chinese Communists after the New Fourth Army Incident and portrays American aid as the force holding their coalition together. It recounts missions by Lauchlin Currie, James Roosevelt, Clarence E. Gauss, Owen Lattimore, and General Magruder, along with financial, military, and transportation assistance. The article concludes that the temporary Anglo-American-Soviet alignment and China's defeat in Hunan expose fundamental weakness in Chongqing-Yan'an resistance.

subfiles.title: Bangkok Prepares to Meet Invaders, Bolsters Defenses
subfiles.from: Domei and the Tokyo Nichi Nichi, published in the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Describes Thai defense preparations while accusing Britain of economic and military pressure on Thailand.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reports Thai air-raid precautions, frontier defenses, mobilization, labor measures, and declarations of neutrality following Japanese moves into French Indochina and the Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran. A parallel report argues that Britain uses oil, gunny bags, trade, troops, railways, and political influence to draw Thailand into the ABCD encirclement of Japan. It names several Thai officials and stresses British financial and educational influence within the country.

subfiles.title: Thai Astride Fence on Issue of Japan
subfiles.from: Japan Advertiser, citing the Bangkok correspondent of the Nichi Nichi
subfiles.about: Warns that British and American propaganda is weakening Thailand's friendship with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The correspondent argues that Japan must wage a stronger propaganda campaign in Thailand following its move into southern French Indochina. British and American reactions to Thailand's recognition of Manchukuo are said to have forced Bangkok to emphasize neutrality. The article particularly alleges British influence over English- and Thai-language newspapers and links it to cooling Thai attitudes toward Japan.

subfiles.title: Settlement in Yen Aim of New Policy
subfiles.from: Japan Advertiser, summarizing an article by Takeo Haraguchi in Diamond
subfiles.about: Advocates a yen-based trading and payments system within the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.
subfiles.summary: Haraguchi traces the tightening of American export controls, the freezing of Japanese assets, and wartime changes in the international roles of the dollar and pound. He argues that Japan should redirect trade away from British and American currency markets and expand exchange with French Indochina, Thailand, and other non-dollar areas. Settlement in yen is presented as essential to Japanese economic leadership in East Asia.

subfiles.title: Japan Will Advance Southward
subfiles.about: Threatens further Japanese southward expansion while demanding British and American withdrawal from East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The article interprets the Roosevelt-Churchill Atlantic meeting as an attempt to halt Japan and protect Anglo-American interests in the Pacific. It argues that Britain and the United States, rather than Japan, are the imperial aggressors in East Asia and demands their withdrawal from India, Burma, Malaya, Hong Kong, China, the Philippines, Guam, and the western Pacific. Japan's prospective southward advance is justified as necessary to establish an East Asian common-prosperity sphere.
